title: Telling a story with a solo
summary: Cootie describes shaping a solo like telling a story, with a statement, a release, and a built second chorus.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yeah. Yeah. Well, Cootie, because -- it's a funny thing, but the two styles that you've got, both styles, nobody ever really did either of them before. And I don't know whether anybody ever did them afterwards. But, first of all, we don't have to elaborate on the point that nobody played the plunger style like you. You didn't play it like Bubber anyway. And what you worked out for yourself -- Tricky Sam was an inspiration, but what you worked out was your thing. And that was that. But the way -- take, like "Concerto for Cootie". You do play open on there, don't you?
Yes, I do.

That's what I thought. Well, nobody ever -- first of all, I guess -- I don't think anybody ever had such a powerful tone. I don't think anybody ever got up and blew so strong, which was also playing jazz, not just playing a straight lead.
No.
Right?
That's right. Uh-huh.
I mean, in other words, it was like --
like playing jazz solo, which came out as strong and pure and beautiful as a first part in a way, but it was also playing jazz. That's a fact, isn't it?
Yeah. Uh-huh.

And so that that becomes -- because this was what was so impressive on that "Concerto for Cootie", so that you really drove and moved the whole band. That one voice. Everything fell in back of it. That's true, isn't it?

Well, yeah. I try to, you know, tell a story when I'm playing. This part too is very important when you're playing an instrument. And to try to tell the story of what you're playing. It's not just to play the notes.
Well, tell that -- spell that out a bit more.
Just like if you're reading a book and you're telling a story to kids, or something. And when you're playing an instrument, which I try to tell a story, when I'm blowing. In the same way.
You start, making an opening statement.
Yeah.
And from there you push your story forward.
That's right.
And then, from what came there, the next thing follows and leads on.
Uh-huh.
And then, when you get your release, the thing is like a contrast, or a new thought or a sort of thing.
Yeah.
And then, Cootie, so when you're going to play a second chorus, then you have your story, and you start to put more force to it, and more feeling to it really. It builds, doesn't it?
Yeah.

Yeah. Well that, you know, that probably accounts for the fact that more or less everything certainly that you recorded can all be sung. And, in fact, when you hear those numbers, you hear in your ear the things that you blew there.
Yeah.
It's like a song, really.
Uh-huh.
It's jazz, but it is like a song. Am I correct in thinking that?
